subject: chemistry
question_text: Write an essay on s, p, d and f block elements.

verification.note: Chapter 2 is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.53-55), which prints the question, its star rank and a model answer. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only — so the two-book union check is PENDING a second chemistry source. The 2+2+2+2 mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. The book's group counts use the old A/B labels (p-block: IIIA to VIIA and the zero group; d-block: IB to VIIB and VIII as three vertical columns); the card keeps them and adds the modern group numbers. Exceptions the book does not mention (helium sitting over the p-block with an s² configuration; the d-block configurations of Cr and Cu) are left to their own cards rather than loaded into this essay.

page_header: Classification of Elements – Periodic Properties · 8 marks

steps.label: Basis of the classification
lines: Based on the sublevel into which the
electron) enters, the elements are classified
steps.why: The whole essay rests on one idea — where the last electron goes — so stating that basis first tells the examiner every block that follows is defined the same way.
common_mistakes: Starting the four blocks without stating the basis of the classification.
Writing valence electron for differentiating electron. The differentiating electron is the last one added.
steps.memory_tip: One question sorts every element: which sublevel did the last electron enter?
steps.margin_note: An opening line, not a marked point — the eight marks sit on the four blocks below.

steps.label: Position sketch
steps.why: Each block's answer says where it lies — left, right, middle, bottom — and one small sketch shows all four positions at once instead of four separate sentences being imagined.
common_mistakes: Placing the d-block at the edge. It sits between the s-block and the p-block.
Attaching the f-block to the main table. It is drawn separately at the bottom.
steps.memory_tip: Left, middle, right, bottom: s, d, p across the table and f below it.
steps.margin_note: An unmarked sketch, but it makes the four position sentences below checkable at a glance.

steps.label: s-block
lines: An s orbital holds two electrons, so the
s-block has two groups: IA and IIA
They lie on the left side of the periodic
table; they are metals and form ionic
steps.why: The group count is not memorised, it is computed: an s orbital holds at most two electrons, so exactly two columns of the table fill it. The same electron-capacity argument gives every block's group count.
common_mistakes: Writing the configuration as ns² only. Group IA has ns¹, so the range is ns¹⁻².
Leaving out either the position or the property. Each block needs its place and one property.
steps.memory_tip: Two electrons fit in s, so two groups: the alkali and alkaline earth metals.
steps.margin_note: Same four lines for every block: where the electron goes, the configuration, the groups, the position with a property.

steps.label: p-block
lines: The p orbitals hold six electrons, so the
p-block has six groups: IIIA to VIIA and the
They lie on the right side of the table; most
are non-metals and form covalent compounds.
steps.why: Six electrons fit in the three p orbitals, so six columns fill them — from np¹ at group IIIA to the complete np⁶ of the noble gases in the zero group.
common_mistakes: Counting five groups by stopping at VIIA. The zero group (noble gases, np⁶) belongs to the p-block.
Writing that all p-block elements are non-metals. Most are; the block also holds metalloids and metals such as Al, Sn and Pb.
steps.memory_tip: Six seats in the p orbitals, six groups, ending at the noble gases with all six filled.
steps.margin_note: The word most before non-metals is deliberate; the block is mixed.

steps.label: d-block
lines: The d orbitals hold ten electrons, so the
d-block has ten groups: IB to VIIB and VIII
They lie in the middle of the table and show
steps.why: Penultimate means last but one: the d electrons enter the shell inside the outermost one, which is why these metals sit between the s- and p-blocks and share properties across the row.
common_mistakes: Writing outermost d orbital. The d electrons enter the penultimate, (n−1), shell.
Counting eight groups by treating VIII as one. VIII spans three vertical columns, giving ten in all.
steps.memory_tip: Ten seats in the d orbitals, ten columns in the middle of the table.
steps.margin_note: Variable oxidation states links this block to the short answer question on transition elements.

steps.label: f-block
lines: The 4f series is the lanthanide series and
the 5f series is the actinide series.
They are placed separately at the bottom of
steps.why: Anti-penultimate means two shells inside the outermost: the f electrons lie deep inside the atom, which is why the fourteen elements of each series are so alike and are placed in two rows below the main table.
common_mistakes: Writing (n−1)f for the configuration. The f electrons enter the (n−2) shell.
Swapping the series names. 4f is the lanthanides, 5f the actinides.
steps.memory_tip: s outermost, d one shell in, f two shells in — each block one level deeper than the last.
steps.margin_note: The boxed configuration is the hardest line of the essay; writing it correctly is what distinguishes the answer.

insider_note: Examiners mark this essay two marks a block, and the same four lines answer each one — where the differentiating electron enters, the general configuration, the number of groups with the reason, and the position with one property.
